content: Instances of disrespectful and abusive treatment during childbirth in healthcare facilities have included physical abuse, severe humiliation, verbal abuse, coercive or forced medical procedures (such as sterilization), breaches of confidentiality, failure to obtain fully informed consent, denial of pain relief, gross violations of privacy, refusal of admission to healthcare facilities, neglect of women during childbirth (a critical time when life-threatening but preventable complications may arise), and detention of women and their newborns in facilities due to inability to pay. Certain groups, including adolescents, unmarried women, women of low socioeconomic status, women from ethnic minorities, migrant women, and women living with HIV, are particularly vulnerable to experiencing disrespectful and abusive treatment during childbirth. To ensure a high standard of respectful care during childbirth, health systems must be structured and managed in a way that upholds women’s sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and human rights. To globally prevent and eliminate disrespect and abuse during facility-based childbirth, the following actions are recommended: 1. Increase support from governments and development partners for research and action addressing disrespect and abuse. 2. Develop, support, and sustain programs aimed at improving the quality of maternal healthcare, with a strong emphasis on respectful care as a fundamental component of quality care. 3. Highlight the rights of women to dignified and respectful healthcare throughout pregnancy and childbirth. 4. Collect data on respectful and disrespectful care practices, and establish accountability systems and meaningful professional support. 5. Engage all stakeholders, including women, in efforts to improve care quality and eliminate disrespectful and abusive practices. Women living with HIV who participated in the Global Values and Preferences Survey (GVPS) identified labor and delivery as a time when they may face neglect and discriminatory care due to healthcare workers’ perceptions about HIV. They emphasized the need to educate families, friends, communities, and healthcare providers about the rights of women living with HIV, normalize “positive” pregnancy and childbirth, and ensure that women have the right to care and support without being required to disclose their HIV status to partners. Respondents also acknowledged that healthcare workers can be highly supportive, especially when women living with HIV are well-informed about their choices through access to reliable and up-to-date information on HIV, pregnancy, and transmission. Self-awareness and confidence in one’s decisions were also noted as important factors. Late cord clamping, performed approximately 1–3 minutes after birth, is recommended for all births while initiating essential newborn care. This recommendation applies to all women, including those living with HIV, as there is no evidence that delayed cord clamping increases the risk of HIV transmission from mother to newborn. The proven benefits of delayed cord clamping outweigh any theoretical and unproven risks. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated in all adolescents living with HIV, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. As a priority, ART should be started in adolescents with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) or a CD4 count ≤ 350 cells/mm³. Similarly, ART should be initiated in all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, and continued lifelong. Mothers living with HIV are encouraged to breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue up to 24 months or longer while being fully supported for ART adherence. ART significantly reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission, even in the context of mixed feeding. The use of amniotomy alone to prevent delays in labor is not recommended due to very low-quality evidence. However, amniotomy combined with oxytocin is recommended for treating confirmed delays in labor. These recommendations apply equally to women living with HIV and other women, with specific guidance provided for settings with high HIV prevalence. Perinatal transmission of HIV, also known as vertical or mother-to-child transmission, can occur during pregnancy (intrauterine), labor and delivery (intrapartum), or breastfeeding (postpartum). Prevention strategies focus on reducing maternal viral load through ART during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period. Comprehensive prevention includes primary prevention of HIV acquisition among women of childbearing age, prevention of unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV, prevention of HIV transmission to infants, and provision of appropriate treatment, care, and support to mothers, children, and families. The global community is committed to eliminating perinatal transmission of HIV and syphilis as a public health priority. The initiative to eliminate mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) emphasizes an integrated approach to improving maternal and child health outcomes, ensuring efficient and high-quality services, and providing comprehensive primary care. A human rights-based approach to ART ensures that pregnant or breastfeeding women receive full information and appropriate medical guidance, enabling them to make voluntary choices about therapy initiation, continuation, and adherence. Healthcare workers must support women in addressing their healthcare needs and those of their children. Safe abortion services for women living with HIV should be the same as for all women, offered in a respectful and non-judgmental manner, free of coercion. Women should have access to medical or surgical abortion options, depending on availability, and their choices must be respected. Women living with HIV emphasized the importance of knowing that it is possible to have HIV-free children through access to prevention programs, including advice and support on delivery and infant feeding options, as well as fertility treatments if needed. They also highlighted the need for mental health support and training for healthcare workers to provide relevant services. Gender inequalities can negatively impact the prevention of perinatal transmission. Constructive male engagement, where applicable, can improve communication, shared responsibility for family health, and child health outcomes. However, women should always be consulted about their preferences for partner involvement, and male engagement should never be a condition for accessing services.
